text:
This chapter discusses markets and marketable products for jackfruit. It notes that the ripe fruit's short shelf life and the difficulty of transporting whole, heavy fruit are major constraints on how far jackfruit can practically travel from the farm to reach buyers, which shapes marketing strategy — much jackfruit is sold relatively close to where it is grown, sold whole at local markets or roadside, or sold as prepared, cleaned flesh (segments) rather than whole fruit, which is lighter, easier to transport and store briefly, and lets buyers see and judge fruit quality directly before purchase.

The chapter references Bangkok's fruit market as an example of a larger urban market where jackfruit from surrounding growing areas is bought and sold, and discusses how transport distance and time affect which form of the product (whole fruit versus prepared flesh) is practical to sell into which market. The text notes that fruit intended for more distant markets needs to be harvested less ripe and handled to minimize bruising and spoilage during the added transport time, a point that connects directly to the harvest-timing guidance given in the previous chapter.

The chapter also touches on price variability by variety, fruit quality (flesh type, size, ripeness, freedom from pest damage), and season (with prices generally lower during the peak glut period and higher when supply is more limited), reinforcing the earlier chapters' emphasis on staggering harvest timing as a market strategy, not just an agronomic one.
